markdown.markdown:
The Swiss Mittelland is among the most densely settled and intensively managed landscapes in Central Europe. Roads, railways, urban expansion and intensive agriculture collectively form a network of barriers that fragments natural habitats and restricts the free movement of wildlife across the region. For large mammals, this fragmentation carries serious long-term consequences: reduced population exchange, diminishing genetic diversity and, ultimately, a decline in regional population viability [@fischer2024; @urbina2023]. In a landscape as structurally altered as the Canton of Zurich, restoring meaningful ecological connectivity is therefore an active and ongoing challenge for wildlife managers and spatial planners.

In response, spatial planning frequently relies on targeted structural interventions such as wildlife overpasses and underpasses, whose effectiveness for species like red deer (*Cervus elaphus*) has been documented across Switzerland and neighbouring France [@fischer2024; @urbina2023]. Assessing where such infrastructure is most needed requires spatially explicit connectivity models. Robust frameworks for this purpose have been established and validated at the regional scale by @urbina2023 and, more recently, for the Swiss Mittelland by @fischer2024, producing maps of movement corridors, pinch points and connectivity bottlenecks that can directly guide conservation planning.

## Problem Statement

What these models have not yet addressed is a parallel management challenge. Unlike red deer, the wild boar (*Sus scrofa*) is not primarily a species in need of connectivity enhancement. It is the primary wildlife reservoir of African Swine Fever (ASF), a viral disease with a case fatality rate of 90 to 95 percent in infected animals for which no effective vaccine exists [@guberti2019]. High landscape connectivity for wild boar directly facilitates the geographic spread of ASF, meaning that interventions designed to benefit species like red deer can simultaneously increase disease transmission risk for wild boar across the same landscape.

This conflict between promoting connectivity for conservation and restricting it to prevent disease spread is not new to ecological theory. @hess1994 demonstrated formally that conservation corridors can, under certain epidemiological conditions, dramatically increase the risk of disease-driven population extinction. The epidemiology of ASF in wild boar matches those conditions closely enough to make this trade-off a concrete management problem for wildlife authorities, particularly as ASF continues to expand its range westward across Europe.

The connectivity models developed by @fischer2024 and @urbina2023 are methodologically rigorous and well validated, but they are static representations of the current landscape. They do not allow practitioners to test hypothetical scenarios interactively. A wildlife manager or veterinary authority asking what would happen to ASF spread risk if a fence were installed along a specific road, or what connectivity a proposed wildlife overpass would deliver for red deer, currently has no tool to answer that question dynamically. This gap between analytical capability and operational decision support is the direct motivation for this thesis.

## Objectives

This thesis develops an interactive spatial planning tool in the form of a QGIS plugin that models functional connectivity for wild boar across the Canton of Zurich. The plugin allows users to dynamically alter the underlying landscape resistance surface by placing hypothetical infrastructure elements, such as movement barriers or wildlife crossings, directly on the map. After each modification, the model recalculates the resulting connectivity and visualises the effect on potential ASF spread corridors and pinch points. The underlying methodology adapts the resistance surface construction, least-cost path calculation and circuit-theory-based corridor modeling approach of @fischer2024 and @urbina2023, with all parameters specifically tailored to the ecology and movement behaviour of wild boar.

Two specific objectives guide this work. The first is the methodological adaptation of the existing connectivity modeling framework for wild boar, including the classification of wild boar telemetry data into in-matrix and in-patch movement, the fitting of an integrated Step Selection Function based on spatial covariantes and finally the construction of a species-specific resistance surface. The second is the development of an interactive QGIS plugin that allows end users to simulate ASF spread from a specific location with different connectivity models and structural landscape changes without requiring programming knowledge.
